text: You're given an integer array called nums. You start at index zero. Each value, nums at i, is the maximum jump length from index i. Return true if you can reach the last index, and false otherwise.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — from index i, I can jump any distance from one up to nums at i, not only exactly that value. I only jump forward. And I just need a yes or no. I don't need the number of jumps, or the actual path. Is that right?
Yes. Any length up to the max, forward only, and just true or false.

Okay. Then there's one fact I want to say early. If I can reach some index j, I can reach every index before j too, because the jump that lands on j could just stop shorter. So the set of reachable indices is always a prefix, from zero up to some farthest point. That means I don't need to track a whole set. One number is enough: how far the prefix goes. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The length is between one and ten to the fourth, and every value is between zero and ten to the fifth.

Got it. So n is at least one, and a single element means I'm already on the last index — true. Zeros are the only thing that can block me. The biggest sum I compute is i plus nums at i, at most nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine plus one hundred thousand — tiny for an int. On the examples: two, three, one, one, four is true, because index one jumps three, straight to the end. Three, two, one, zero, four is false — every index before the zero can reach index three and no further, and the zero there is a wall.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach treats it as a graph and runs a breadth-first search, or a dynamic program over reachable indices. That's correct, and I'd keep it as a checker, but it touches every edge, so it can be quadratic — wasted work with jumps up to a hundred thousand. This problem reminds me of a greedy frontier scan — a running-maximum sweep over one growing covered interval, the same idea as merging overlapping intervals into a single covered prefix. Because the reachable set is a prefix, I only push its right edge forward: each index inside it offers i plus nums at i, and I take the max. One pass, no set, no queue.

Here's the plan. One: keep farthest, the right edge of the reachable prefix using only earlier indices, starting at zero. Two: for each index, if i is beyond farthest, nobody before i reaches it, and since the set is a prefix, nothing after it either — return false. Three: otherwise push farthest to the max of itself and i plus nums at i; if the loop finishes, return true. One thing worth flagging — the check must come before the update. Update first, and farthest is always at least i, so the check never fires and the function never returns false — even on example two. There's a trade-off here. A backward version moves a goal down from the last index; it's also linear and correct, but forward stops early at the first wall. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop over the indices: first the check, if i is greater than farthest, return false; then farthest becomes the max of itself and i plus nums at i. After the loop, return true. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — the compare is strictly greater. When i equals farthest, I'm standing on the last reachable index, which is fine; greater-or-equal would return false at index zero for every input, even a single zero. And the max is needed: assigning i plus nums at i directly lets a small value pull the edge back. On two, zero, zero, that returns false instead of true — yet it passes both official examples.

Let's dry-run the code with example two — three, two, one, zero, four — expected false. Indices zero through three all offer exactly three, so farthest is stuck at three. The row that matters is i equals four: four is greater than three, so I return false right there. The zero at index three is the wall. Example one, by contrast, reaches four by index one, and at the end four is not greater than four, so true. That matches. Corner cases: a single zero is true — I'm already there. Zero then one is false, stuck at index zero. Two, zero, zero is true, reaching the end exactly. And one, zero, one, zero is false — the one at index two never helps, because I never reach it.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — one compare and one max per index. Space is constant — two integers. The worst false case is all ones with a zero just before the end, so the wall is found only at the last index, after all ten thousand steps — about eight microseconds. Farthest never goes above about one hundred ten thousand, so a plain int is safe. Oh, one more thing — I'd test this against the breadth-first-search checker. I ran every array of length one to eight with values zero to three, plus random large ones — over three hundred thousand cases, zero mismatches. The same test shows how the bugs fail: update-before-check fails exactly the false arrays, greater-or-equal fails exactly the true arrays, and dropping the max fails about twenty-eight thousand cases while still passing both official examples.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw early that the reachable set is always a prefix, so one number, farthest, replaces the whole breadth-first search. You explained why the check must come before the update, and why it's strictly greater and not greater or equal — one bug never says false, the other always does. And you showed the max is a correctness need, with two, zero, zero — a case both official examples miss. Good work.
